chapter_theme: Natrinai 101 to 120: the hill tryst under threat of night paths, traps and confinement; the shore's evenings and returns; the man on the road for wealth held back by memory; and in two marutham and household poems the wife's hidden strength, in poverty and in the sulk a guest dissolves.

101.reading: The man, within the friend's hearing, says the shore hamlet where curled prawns are heaped to dry in the punnai's shade was a sweet place to live, until he saw the deer-like look of the fisherman's young daughter.
101.nuance: The whole poem is a before and after: the busy, pleasant work of the shore is described only to be lost, and the loss is dated to one sight of her eyes; spoken where the friend can hear, it is his plea for her help.

thinai_evidence.note: prawns, the punnai shade and the fishermen fix the shore

comparisons.tenor: the rough skins of the curled prawns

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he speaks to no one named; the colophon says the friend hears

102.reading: The woman begs the red-beaked parrot, with joined hands, to eat its fill of the millet without fear and then, when it goes to its kin on his jackfruit slopes, to tell the lord of that hill that the young daughter of this hill's kuravar has been set to guard the millet.
102.nuance: She strikes a bargain with the very bird she is posted to drive away: it may eat the crop if it carries her message, and the message itself (she is at the field by day) is the invitation.

thinai_evidence.note: parrot, jackfruit slope, hill hunters and millet are of the hill

103.reading: Midway on the road for wealth, the man tells his heart to decide one thing: in this strange hot forest, where a hungry red she-dog with dried teats lies curled on ground wet with no water and her mate, gone on his unfailing hunt, grieves thinking of her, we suffer; whether we go on for our work or turn back, it is your choice.
103.nuance: The wild dogs are a couple split by hunger exactly as he and his wife are split by the hunt for wealth; the male who has gone to hunt yet grieves for his mate is the man himself, so the heart's choice is already answered by the scene.

thinai_evidence.note: a man on the road away from his wife, in the burning waste

iraicchi.act: the male wild dog, gone on a hunt, grieves remembering his mate who lies starving
iraicchi.sense: the man who has left on his own hunt for wealth is bound to grieve for his wife in the same way, so the heart should turn back

104.reading: The woman asks whether anyone but she, who lives loving the chest of the lord of the loud hill where hill boys beat drums at a tiger fighting a tusker and others scare parrots off the millet, ever thinks of the narrow, hard-to-see path he takes at midnight, when thunder strikes the snake-holed hill and the flood blocks the way.
104.nuance: The hill's children turn the tiger-elephant fight into a game for their drums, fearless; she is the one person on that hill who is afraid, and the fear is for him.

thinai_evidence.note: tiger, millet, the hill lord and the midnight tryst

105.reading: The man scolds his heart, which wants to turn back midway: it never weighed the forked tracks of this shadeless, waterless waste where hot wind shakes the thorny silk-cotton and an elephant suffers with its calf, and now it has come far only to pine for her soft hair, fragrant as the bee-visited kuvalai of the springs on Kuttuvan's western hill.
105.nuance: The rebuke is double-edged: the heart is blamed for not foreseeing the road, but its real fault is that it already turns home to her, and the one rich image in the waste is her hair.

colophon.thurai: இடைச் சுரத்து மீளலுற்ற நெஞ்சினைத் தலைமகன் கழறியது

thinai_evidence.note: the waterless, shadeless track

106.reading: Turning back as the season brings a past moment to mind, the man asks his charioteer whether he knows how, on the wave-heaped dune where the striped crab ran and she, unable to keep up, stayed behind, he went and told her his inner pain, and she, unable to answer, pulled down the gnaazhal's hanging cluster and crushed its sprouts till they fell from her hand, lost in her shy distress.
106.nuance: Her answer to his first confession is a gesture, not a word: her hand tearing at the flowering branch says what her mouth cannot, and it is this silence, not any speech, that calls him home.

colophon.thurai: பருவ வரவின்கண் பண்டு நிகழ்ந்ததோர் குறிப்பு உணர்ந்த தலைவன் அதனைக் கண்டு தாங்ககில்லானாய் மீள்கின்றான் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச்சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: sea, dune, crab and gnaazhal are of the shore

107.reading: The wasting woman tells her friend that she laughs whenever she thinks of it: her heart, which went with her lover along the tiger-haunted track of omai trees where dry paalai pods rattle in the wind like a waterfall, has the good share, while she, left here wearing endless gossip, has the share of pain.
107.nuance: She divides herself in two and envies the half that left; the laughter is at her own lot, and the pod simile (like the pincer-shaped stalk a she-elephant splits) turns on rare words.

thinai_evidence.note: the paalai tree, omai and the tiger's track

comparisons.tenor: the rattle of the pods in the wind
her heart that went and herself who stayed

108.reading: The friend tells the lord of the land where hill folk, with arrows, drums and slings, shout from the village edge at a fierce elephant parted from its mate as it nears the millet: even parting from a familiar enemy hurts; how could he let go the bond while this girl with bud-like teeth and flame-bright brow turns pale; she grieves for it.
108.nuance: The proverb at the turn (பழகிய பகையும் பிரிவு இன்னாதே) shames him: parting from a known foe is hard, and he parts lightly from a lover.

colophon.thurai: வரையாது நெடுங் காலம்வந்து ஒழுகலாற்றாளாய தோழி தலைமகளது ஆற்றாமை கூறி வரைவு கடாயது

thinai_evidence.note: millet beside the hill, the elephant and the hill hunters

ullurai.tenor: the lover who keeps coming unmarried and the watchful village

pairs.situation: he goes about without the partner he has not wed
his stealthy approach to the girl by night
the clamour and watch of the village that make secret visits dangerous

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the hill's elephant and hunters in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

109.reading: The woman answers her friend, who keeps asking whether this is her state now that the lover of old friendship, who promised they would be one, has gone: listen; her sorrow cannot be told; as the evening passes with the north wind humming in the dark, she stands alone and turning, like a cow tied by the head in a dripping shed.
109.nuance: The simile is exact about helplessness: the tied cow in the cold shed cannot move to shelter or to its calf, as she can neither go to him nor stop waiting.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகளது நிலைகண்ட தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: a wife waiting through the cold evening, with the cattle shed and north wind

110.reading: Wondering at a daughter's household, the speaker recalls the little girl who ran, gold anklets ringing, under the pandal to refuse the honeyed milk her old nurses chased her with, and asks where she learned this sense and conduct: now that her husband's family has fallen poor, she does not think of the rich rice her father sends, and eats only at alternate meals, small and strong-willed.
110.nuance: The poem rests on the gap between the two pictures, the spoilt child who would not eat and the wife who will not eat more than her husband's house can give; the closing simile of the fine ripples in flowing water is obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife's steadfast keeping of her husband's house; no land is named

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: speaker and addressee inferred; the colophon names neither

111.reading: The friend, glad at a good omen, tells the woman that to the great backwater hamlet, loud as the fisher boys come down the sloping sand with boats full of fat after crossing the wave-desert on their catamarans, like young hunters setting out for deer, to catch swordfish and prawns with heads like iruppai flowers, the lord's chariot is coming.
111.nuance: The fleet's noisy homecoming is the sound that announces the chariot; the fishermen's sea is drawn as a paalai waste (திரைச் சுரம்) and their fishing as a deer hunt.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen, catamarans, sharks and the backwater hamlet

comparisons.tenor: the fisher boys setting out to sea

112.reading: The friend asks what feast she can give this rain-cloud that, knowing the coming of the lord of the great-rock land where vengai has bloomed and a fearless lion kills an elephant, has gladly scooped the dark sea, poured down the sapphire falls and flashes like the mountain blinking, packed with strong thunder.
112.nuance: She turns the rain, which the waiting woman dreads as a sign of broken time, into a guest who has come ahead of him, and the joke of feasting a cloud is her way of making the heroine smile.

thinai_evidence.note: vengai, lion and the land of great rocks

113.reading: Unable to go on in the wilds, the man says that though he has crossed the great forest where green iratthi pods, nibbled by deer, lie strewn on the stony path, her look has come with him: when he said he would go after hard-won wealth, she hid her neythal eyes in her long hair, broken, and sobbed like the ambal pipe the musicians blow on the hushed field after Udhiyan's loud battle.
113.nuance: The sob is likened not to a lament but to the pipe played on a battlefield after the fighting, so her one moment of grief carries the hush of a field of the dead.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has crossed the forest in pursuit of wealth

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: he speaks to himself

114.reading: With the man nearby, the friend tells the woman that, awake all night, she heard the hamlet's noise as white tusks were laid on the rock and raw meat cut, and was troubled: he surely came last night, the hill lord, and she fears the river that rises in waves against its rain-pitted banks, and the thunder that struck the tusker coming down the high hill, leaving the young she-elephant grieving.
114.nuance: The hamlet's feast on a killed elephant and the thunder that kills another frame the night path as a place where tuskers die; she says it to the heroine but means him to hear.

colophon.thurai: ஆறு பார்த்து உற்ற அச்சத்தால் தோழி தலைவிக்கு உரைப்பாளாய் சிறைப்புறமாகச் சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: the hill lord, elephants and the small hill hamlet

iraicchi.act: the young she-elephant is left bewildered and grieving when the thunder strikes her tusker on the path down the hill
iraicchi.sense: the heroine would be left the same way if the man keeps taking the night path, so he should stop coming by night

115.reading: The friend tells the woman that the rains have come this morning, the peacock-foot leaved nocchi and the jasmine in the yard opening their buds, so that her tired playmates may sleep and even mother breathes easier; though her lover is in a far country he has very great love, and would not stay away even for endless fame: has she not heard what the sky's keeping of time shows?
115.nuance: The proof is the sky itself: the rains have kept their season, and the friend asks her to read his promise by it; the last words set love above the one thing puram men are praised for seeking, fame.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை ஆற்றாளாய தலைமகளைத் தோழி பருவம் காட்டி வற்புறுத்தியது

thinai_evidence.note: the rains' coming and the jasmine

116.reading: Refusing her friend's comfort, the woman says the great say one should understand even those who wrong us; the friendship of the hill lord, where a pregnant young she-elephant grazes on bamboo shoots, has broken off and gone far, like a ripe jackfruit that leaves its branch and bursts in a rock cleft, yet the women of the kurinji town, not knowing that, still keep up their gossip about her.
116.nuance: The bitterness is that the gossip outlives the love it was about: the bond has burst like the fallen fruit, but the town's talk goes on; the opening maxim is hard to construe.

colophon.thurai: வரைவு நீட்டிப்ப ஆற்றாளாய தலைவி தோழிக்கு வன்புறை எதிரழிந்து சொல்லியது

thinai_evidence.note: elephant, jackfruit and the kurinji town

comparisons.vehicle: பலவின் மாச் சினை துறந்த கோள் முதிர் பெரும் பழம்

117.reading: Refusing comfort, the woman tells her friend that in the sorrowful evening, when the sea roars, the tide overflows the houses, the neythal closes, birds go together to their nests and the reddened sun sinks to the hill, he does not think of her, and she will not live many days; people call her sickness something else, and it is not right that the blame should fall elsewhere either.
117.nuance: The closing lines turn from grief to a sharper point: if her love-sickness is taken for something else, the man escapes the blame, and she will not let him.

colophon.thurai: வரைவு நீட ஆற்றாளாய தலைவி வன்புறை எதிரழிந்து சொல்லியது சிறைப்புறமும்ஆம்

thinai_evidence.note: the shore at sunset

iraicchi.act: the birds go together to their nests in the grove at evening
iraicchi.sense: even the birds come home together at dusk, while he does not come or think of her

118.reading: The woman says that even in the flowering season, when the red-eyed koel with its mate calls back eagerly from the mango boughs on the bank, she thinks he who left has surely forgotten them; and beyond that, her heart aches at the stranger woman who goes street by street crying new pathiri flowers, fluffy-tipped like a painter's brush dipped in lac.
118.nuance: The flower-seller is a stranger to her grief and that is the wound: the season is being sold cheerfully in every street, and she must hear it.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman left behind in the spring by a man gone away

comparisons.vehicle: ஓவ மாக்கள் ஒள் அரக்கு ஊட்டிய துகிலிகை

iraicchi.act: the koel, together with its mate, calls back eagerly in the flowering season
iraicchi.sense: in the season when even the koel is with its mate, the man who left has failed to come, so she reads it as his forgetting

119.reading: With the man listening, the friend says that the lord of the land where a hill farmer's stone trap, set for the millet-eating boar, catches a bright strong tiger, though he came to have his fill, will come to the shade of the great hill beyond the flowered forest river, where langurs and stags leap with wild goats, wearing kulavi and kuuthalam, and will not get a single embrace; let his sulking be greater than his mountain.
119.nuance: She tells him that the girl is now shut in the house: he will come to the usual place in his hill garland and find no one.

thinai_evidence.note: millet, boar, tiger and hill flowers

ullurai.tenor: the lover and the girl's family who have shut her in

pairs.scene: சிறு பொறி மாட்டிய பெருங் கல் அடாஅர்
pairs.situation: the family's confinement of the girl, set against intruders
the strong lover himself is caught and foiled by it

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the hill farmer's trap and tiger in a kurinji poem (porul 7.27)

120.reading: Having come in with a guest as his way in, the man says that in the fine house where buffalo calves are tied to every pillar, his young wife, her soft fingers reddening as she cuts wet slices of vaalai fish, eyes smarting with smoke, wiping the sweat from her crescent brow with her garment's edge and sulking at him, is in the kitchen; let guests come to them, for she will not be angry then, and he will see her face smile with small sharp teeth showing.
120.nuance: The guest is his weapon in the quarrel: hospitality forbids her a sour face, so the man who caused the sulk can count on her smile.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's sulking, with buffalo and vaalai fish of the fields

links.note: Both are the man struck by the girl's look and both find a doe in it: Kural 1085 asks whether her look is Death, an eye or a doe; Natrinai 101 says the shore hamlet was sweet to live in before he saw her deer-like look.
links.teaches: The couplet says what the look contains, the doe beside Death; the Natrinai man shows what Death in it did, measuring the wound as the loss of his home's sweetness from the day he saw her.

links.note: In both the heroine sends the hill lord word that she has been set to guard the millet against parrots: in Kuruntokai 141 through the friend, with a warning not to come at midnight, in Natrinai 102 through a parrot itself.
links.teaches: The millet-guard message was a fixed kalavu signal meaning she can be met by day, and Natrinai turns the crop's enemy into its carrier, so the bird she is posted to chase becomes the go-between she bribes with the crop.

links.note: Both put a drought-starved animal couple on the man's road for wealth: in Akananuru 91 the friend cites the elephant shrinking beside his hungry mate to assure the wife of his love; in Natrinai 103 the man himself sees the male wild dog grieving for his starving mate.
links.teaches: The image the friend offers the wife as reassurance is the one the man meets as self-reproach on the road, so the pair shows the same iraicchi working from both ends of the separation, comfort at home and conscience in the waste.

links.note: Akananuru 91 says the man would not stay away even if he gained Kuttuvan's rich Kudanadu; in Natrinai 105 the man's heart, midway on the road, turns back to her hair, fragrant as the kuvalai of Kuttuvan's western hill.
links.teaches: What the friend in Akananuru 91 asserts from outside, that Kuttuvan's whole land would not hold him, Natrinai 105 shows from inside his heart, where Kuttuvan's country survives only as a measure of her fragrance.

links.note: Both have the woman's heart following the man who has left; Kural 1248 calls the heart a fool for going after him, Natrinai 107 says the heart that went has the good share and she who stayed has the pain.
links.teaches: The same split between a heart that follows and a self left behind is judged in opposite ways: Valluvar's woman despises the following heart, the Natrinai woman envies it, because she is the one left to bear the town's gossip.

links.note: Both are the separated woman at evening in a pastoral scene: in Kural 1228 the herdsman's flute is the burning evening's messenger and a killing weapon; in Natrinai 109 she stands alone like a cow tied by the head in a dripping shed.
links.teaches: The pastoral evening gives the Kural woman a sound that attacks her and the Natrinai woman a posture she shares, so the mullai hour wounds in one from outside and in the other makes her one of its own tethered creatures.

links.note: Kural 51 defines the wife as one who lives within the means of the man who took her; Natrinai 110 shows a spoilt girl who once refused honeyed milk now eating only at alternate meals in her husband's poor house, refusing her rich father's food.
links.teaches: The poem shows what the couplet's rule costs and how strange it looks to her own family, who ask where she learned it, so living within his means appears as a change of person rather than a skill.

links.note: Purananuru 2 praises Udhiyan Cheralathan for the great food he gave at the war of the hundred and the five; Natrinai 113 likens the heroine's sob to the ambal pipe the musicians blow on the hushed field after Udhiyan's loud battle.
links.teaches: Where the praise poem remembers Udhiyan's war for its feeding of the armies, the love poet remembers its aftermath, the silent field and the mourning pipe, so akam took from the same king's fame the grief that puram praise leaves out.

links.note: Both paalai poems use Udhiyan Cheral's great occasions as similes: Akananuru 233 compares the crowded hills of the man's road to the ghouls gathered at Udhiyan's great feast; Natrinai 113 compares the left wife's sob to the pipe blown after Udhiyan's battle.
links.teaches: Held together they show akam poets dividing one king's famous scenes between the two halves of separation, his feast for the harsh road the man crosses and his battlefield's lament for the woman he leaves.

links.note: Both have the friend fearing the man's night path, where storms strike down snakes on the hill; Akananuru 182 tells him directly to come by day, Natrinai 114 speaks to the heroine within his hearing and adds the thunder-killed tusker and his grieving mate.
links.teaches: The pair shows the two routes of the same warning: the direct plea in Akananuru 182, and in Natrinai 114 the overheard speech that lets the friend show him, through the she-elephant, what his death would leave behind without telling him what to do.

links.note: Purananuru 182 says the world stands because there are men who would give their lives for fame; Natrinai 115 says the absent lover, of great love, would not stay away even for endless fame.
links.teaches: On one defensible reading the two rank the same goods in opposite order, puram putting fame above life and akam putting love above fame, so the friend's comfort works only by overturning the heroic scale the puram poem praises.

links.note: Both are the friend comforting the wife with the same formula, that the man has very great love (பெரும்பேர் அன்பினர், மிகப் பேர் அன்பினர்) and would not stay even if he gained something: Kuttuvan's land in Akananuru 91, endless fame in Natrinai 115.
links.teaches: The comfort is a fixed frame whose slot each poet fills with the highest prize of the puram world, land in one and fame in the other, so the formula is a measure of love against the goods of war.

links.note: Both are the deserted woman facing the town's gossip: in Kural 1149 she asks how she can be ashamed of gossip when the man who told her not to fear has left her; in Natrinai 116 the bond has burst like a fallen jackfruit yet the women still keep up their talk of her.
links.teaches: In the Kural his leaving cancels the shame of the gossip, while in Natrinai the gossip outlives the bond it was about, so the pair shows two answers to the same abandonment: indifference to talk or bearing talk about a love that is already gone.

links.note: Both are the woman's love-sickness at evening in separation: Kural 1227 says the sickness buds at morning, grows through the day and blooms at evening; Natrinai 117 sets her evening on the shore, where the neythal closes and birds go home together while he does not think of her.
links.teaches: Set beside the shore's evening, where the neythal shuts, the couplet's sickness that blooms at evening reads as the one flower that opens when the others close, and the poem supplies the scene the couplet compresses into a single growth.

links.note: Kural 90 says a guest withers when the host's face changes; in Natrinai 120 the man brings a guest into the house because his sulking wife will not show an angry face to a guest and he will see her smile.
links.teaches: The rule of the welcoming face that the Kural lays on the host becomes, in the poem, the husband's lever against the wife's sulk, so the guest is both the object of hospitality and the akam go-between (வாயில்) that ends an oodal.

source_issues: 108: the colophon heading gives no poet and no '(?)' (text flag).
119: lines 7 and 8 carry the -ஒடு vowel sign restored from sangamtamil.com (text flags).
109: the colophon thinai is பாலை; the poem has the cold north wind, evening and the cattle shed of a waiting wife, and I infer mullai (irutthal).

110: the colophon thinai is பாலை and its thurai names no speaker; the poem names no land, and I infer mullai from the wife's steadfast household conduct, with the speaker inferred as the foster mother.

115: lines 3 and 4 (இன் நீர்த் தடங் கடல் வாயில் உண்டு சில் நீர் என) are hard to construe; 116: the opening maxim (lines 1 to 3, வழுவப் பிண்டம்) is obscure; 114: lines 1 to 4 (முணக்கவும், பையாந்திசினே) are uncertain.
Natrinai colophons name the speaker and occasion but rarely the addressee; addressees marked as inferred are mine.
